n: Why is my eyelid twitching?
a: Usually from tiredness, stress or caffeine, and it goes away on its own. If it lasts for weeks or spreads to the face, see a doctor.

n: How do I prevent falls in older adults?
a: Tai chi and balance exercises, a review of medicines and eyesight, good lighting at home.

n: Does intermittent fasting work?
a: You lose as much weight as with simple calorie reduction. It helps people who find it easy.

n: Do fat burners work?
a: They have no meaningful benefit and some have caused serious harm. Weight loss comes from diet and movement.

n: I always feel tired. Which tests should I get?
a: Full blood count, ferritin, B12, thyroid, blood sugar, vitamin D. Also consider sleep (apnoea), mood and medicines.

n: What should I do about fatty liver?
a: Lose 7–10% of your weight, exercise, less sugar and alcohol. Avoid "detox" herbs.

n: Iron makes me constipated. What do I do?
a: Try iron bisglycinate, taking it every other day or with a little food. Black stools are expected.

n: Should I take iron if I feel tired?
a: Not without tests. With thalassaemia or haemochromatosis, iron is harmful. Measure ferritin and a full blood count first.

n: How should I take iron for better absorption?
a: On an empty stomach or with a little food, with vitamin C or an orange, away from coffee, tea, milk and calcium. Taking it every other day increases absorption.

n: What helps male fertility?
a: Quitting smoking, a normal weight, less alcohol, avoiding anabolic steroids. Supplements have limited evidence.

n: How much fibre do I need?
a: 25–30 g a day. Increase gradually and drink water so you do not get bloated.

n: How much fish should I eat because of mercury?
a: 2 portions a week, mainly small fish (sardines, anchovies). In pregnancy, avoid swordfish and shark.

n: Does omega-3 help ADHD?
a: A small benefit in some studies. It does not replace treatment.

n: When should I start folic acid for pregnancy?
a: At least 1 month before conception and until week 12, 400 µg a day. With epilepsy, diabetes or a previous pregnancy with a defect, the doctor sets a higher dose.

n: Are IgG food intolerance tests worth it?
a: No. They have no proven diagnostic value and can lead to unnecessary restrictions.

n: Are frozen vegetables good?
a: Yes, they keep their nutrients well and are economical.

n: Does fruit have a lot of sugar?
a: The sugar in whole fruit comes with fibre. Fruit is linked with less, not more, diabetes.

n: What should I avoid with favism?
a: Broad beans, naphthalene (mothballs), certain medicines (there is an official list) and very high doses of vitamin C. Always tell your doctor and pharmacist.

n: Is gluten bad for everyone?
a: No. A gluten-free diet is necessary only with coeliac disease, wheat allergy or confirmed sensitivity.

n: What should I avoid with gout?
a: Beer and alcohol, drinks with fructose, a lot of red meat and seafood. Water and weight loss help.

n: Why is grapefruit not allowed with some medicines?
a: It blocks an enzyme in the gut and raises levels of some statins, immunosuppressants and heart medicines. Read the patient leaflet.

n: Is green tea bad for the liver?
a: The drink is not. Extracts in capsules with high EGCG have caused liver damage, especially on an empty stomach.

n: Can grey hair turn dark again?
a: Rarely, only if caused by a deficiency (e.g. B12). It is usually hereditary.

n: How do I improve gut health?
a: A variety of plant foods, fibre, fermented foods. Probiotics help in specific situations.

n: What should I check if my hair is falling out?
a: Ferritin, thyroid, vitamin D and, in women, hormones. After childbirth, fever or stress, hair loss is common and temporary.

n: Is there a hangover cure?
a: None proven. Water between drinks, food beforehand, sleep. Do not take paracetamol after a lot of alcohol.

n: Can dehydration cause a headache?
a: Yes, mild dehydration is linked with headache and worse mood.

n: Is there a supplement for the heart?
a: None replaces medicines. High-dose EPA helps with high triglycerides under a doctor. Vitamin E and beta-carotene did not help.

n: Can I do HIIT at an older age?
a: Yes, with adjusted intensity, and after your doctor approves it if you have heart disease.

n: Does honey help a cough?
a: Yes, in children over 1 year it reduces night-time coughing. Never give it to babies under 1 year.

n: Is there anything that "boosts" the immune system?
a: Sleep, exercise, vaccines and correcting deficiencies (D, zinc). "Immune booster" products have no clear evidence.

n: Should I use iodised salt?
a: Yes, instead of plain salt, but keep the total amount of salt moderate.

n: How do I deal with jet lag?
a: Daylight at your destination at the right times and melatonin 0.5–3 mg at the destination's bedtime.

n: Which supplement helps the joints?
a: Turmeric has relatively the best evidence for knee osteoarthritis. Glucosamine has mixed results. Weight loss and strengthening help more.

n: Is fresh juice the same as fruit?
a: No. Juice has less fibre and a lot of sugar. Choose the whole fruit.

n: Is the ketogenic diet safe?
a: For a short time in healthy people usually yes, but it can raise LDL a lot. Not in type 1 diabetes, pregnancy or with certain medicines.

n: How much water for kidney stones?
a: Enough to pass more than 2–2.5 litres of urine a day. That usually means 2.5–3 litres of fluids.

n: Can I give my child melatonin?
a: Only on a paediatrician's advice. First a steady sleep routine and fewer screens.

n: Do children need vitamins?
a: Most children with a varied diet do not, except vitamin D for babies. Keep gummies out of reach: iron overdose is dangerous.

n: How do I know if I'm lactose intolerant?
a: Bloating or diarrhoea after milk that improves when you avoid it. There is a breath test.

n: Is lemon water in the morning good for you?
a: It is a healthy drink, but it does not "cleanse" or make you lose weight. Rinse your mouth to protect your teeth.

n: Are there supplements for libido?
a: Maca and ginseng have small studies. Avoid products from the internet, which often contain hidden drugs.

n: What helps with long COVID?
a: Pacing your energy and a gradual return to activity with medical follow-up. Supplements have no proven benefit.

n: What really makes a difference to longevity?
a: Not smoking, fitness, strength, a Mediterranean diet, sleep, social ties and blood pressure control. No supplement has been proven to extend life.

n: Does red meat cause cancer?
a: Processed meats are proven carcinogens. Red meat probably is, in large amounts. Limit it to 2–3 times a week.

n: Does meditation work?
a: Moderate improvement in anxiety, depression and pain. Consistency matters more than duration.

n: Should I tell my doctor about supplements?
a: Yes, always, and before surgery. Many interact with medicines.

n: How much melatonin should I take?
a: Start with 0.5–1 mg, 1–2 hours before bed. Larger doses often cause a heavy head in the morning without extra benefit.

n: Is melatonin safe for daily use?
a: It does not cause dependence like sleeping pills, but long-term safety has not been well studied. Small doses (0.5–1 mg) are often enough. For chronic insomnia, CBT-I comes first.

n: How do I improve my memory?
a: Sleep, exercise, social and mental activity, checking hearing and blood pressure. Rule out B12 deficiency.

n: Is hormone therapy safe in menopause?
a: For most healthy women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause, the benefits usually outweigh the risks. The decision is individual.

n: Are there natural remedies for hot flushes?
a: Phytoestrogens have a small benefit and black cohosh probably none. Cognitive behavioural therapy and non-hormonal medicines are alternatives.

n: Does metabolism slow with age?
a: A large study (Science 2021) showed it stays stable from 20 to 60. Muscle loss and moving less matter more.

n: Why check B12 if I take metformin?
a: Long-term metformin reduces B12 absorption and can cause neuropathy. Test once a year.

n: Why does magnesium give me diarrhoea?
a: Oxide and citrate draw water into the gut. Try glycinate or a smaller, split dose.

n: Which form of magnesium is best?
a: Glycinate is gentle on the gut and preferred for sleep. Citrate is well absorbed and helps constipation. Oxide is poorly absorbed and acts mainly as a laxative.

n: When should I take magnesium?
a: Many people take it in the evening for sleep. Keep it 2 hours apart from some antibiotics and 4 hours from thyroxine.

n: Can I take magnesium and zinc together?
a: Yes, at usual doses. Very high doses of zinc (over 40 mg) lower copper.

n: Which supplements help migraine?
a: Magnesium, riboflavin (B2) 400 mg and possibly Q10 for prevention, with results after 2–3 months.

n: Is exercise better in the morning or evening?
a: The best time is the one you can stick to. Hard exercise very close to bedtime makes sleep harder for some people.

n: I have an MTHFR mutation. Do I need methylfolate?
a: The variant is very common and most people respond normally to folic acid. Methylfolate is an alternative, not a necessity.

n: Do I need a multivitamin?
a: If you eat a varied diet, usually not. Useful with a restricted diet, older age or after bariatric surgery. It did not prevent heart disease in large studies.

n: Can I build muscle after 60?
a: Yes. Weight training increases strength and muscle at any age, together with enough protein.

n: Why do my nails break?
a: Often from water and detergents. Check iron and thyroid. Biotin only helps with a deficiency.

n: Are afternoon naps bad?
a: A 10–20 minute nap before 3 pm helps. Longer naps disrupt night-time sleep.

n: If it's natural, is it safe?
a: Not necessarily. Kava, black cohosh and green tea extract have caused liver damage, and St John's wort interacts with many medicines.

n: Is time in nature good for you?
a: 120 minutes a week is linked with better wellbeing.

n: Do nootropics work?
a: Caffeine with theanine has a small proven effect. Most others have very little data.

n: Do nuts make you fat?
a: A handful a day is not linked with weight gain in studies, despite the calories.

n: Can I cook with olive oil?
a: Yes. Virgin olive oil is stable at home cooking temperatures.

n: Omega-3 gives me fishy burps. What do I do?
a: Take them with food, try frozen or enteric-coated capsules, or the triglyceride form.

n: How much omega-3 do I need?
a: For general health 250–500 mg EPA+DHA, which 2 portions of oily fish a week provide. Higher doses (2–4 g) for triglycerides, with a doctor.

n: How do I read an omega-3 label?
a: What matters is EPA+DHA per dose, not the capsule weight. A 1000 mg capsule may contain only 300 mg EPA+DHA.

n: Is organic food healthier?
a: It has fewer pesticide residues, but no meaningful health difference has been proven. Eating more fruit and vegetables matters more.

n: Do I need calcium for my bones?
a: Get it from food first (dairy, sardines, tahini). A supplement if your diet falls short, up to 500 mg per dose.
